hints: Notice that you start with two different halides, so think about the two different silver halide colours that will form together.
X must be a mixture of white $\text{AgCl}$ from the chloride and yellow $\text{AgI}$ from the iodide.
Remember which silver halide dissolves in concentrated ammonia and which one is left behind as the remaining solid.
walkthrough:
**Work out what precipitate X is**

Both sodium salts dissolve to give $\text{Cl}^-$ and $\text{I}^-$ ions. With excess $\text{AgNO}_3$, both precipitate.

$$\text{Ag}^+ + \text{Cl}^- \rightarrow \text{AgCl (white)}$$ $$\text{Ag}^+ + \text{I}^- \rightarrow \text{AgI (yellow)}$$

**Recall solubility in ammonia**

This is the classic halide test. $\text{AgCl}$ dissolves in dilute and concentrated ammonia to form the complex $[\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_3)_2]^+$. $\text{AgBr}$ dissolves only in concentrated ammonia. $\text{AgI}$ is insoluble even in concentrated ammonia.

**Find what precipitate Y is**

When excess concentrated ammonia is added to X, the white $\text{AgCl}$ part dissolves away, but the yellow $\text{AgI}$ part stays solid. So Y is the leftover $\text{AgI}$, which looks yellow.

options.A: X is not pure white. It contains white $\text{AgCl}$ but also yellow $\text{AgI}$, so the mixture looks off-white, cream or pale yellow, not pure white.
options.B: X is not pure $\text{AgI}$. Because the original powder contained both $\text{NaCl}$ and $\text{NaI}$, X is a mixture of $\text{AgCl}$ and $\text{AgI}$.
options.C: Y cannot be pure $\text{AgCl}$. $\text{AgCl}$ dissolves in concentrated ammonia to give soluble $[\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_3)_2]^+$, so it goes into solution and does not remain as a precipitate.
options.D: Y is the $\text{AgI}$ left undissolved after the $\text{AgCl}$ has dissolved in excess concentrated ammonia. $\text{AgI}$ is yellow, so this statement is correct.
